newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Prodi wins mini-budget confidence vote.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Prodi wins mini-budget confidence vote.

text.p: The government comfortably won a confidence vote in parliament on Tuesday called to speed approval of a controversial mini-budget it says is vital to Italy's drive to join Europe's single currency.
The centre-left government won the vote in the Chamber of Deputies (lower house), its 21st such do-or-die measure in a year, by 318 to 260, parliamentary officials said.
The victory, which had been expected, sweeps aside hundreds of opposition amendments to the package, which will pass to the Senate (upper house).
It is designed to trim the 1997 deficit by 15.5 trillion lire ($9 billion) to boost Italy's bid to qualify for economic and monetary union (EMU) at its planned start in January 1999.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi has repeatedly said he will resign if pro-Europe Italy fails to join the single currency.

The mini-budget, the latest dose of bitter medicine dished out by Prodi in the name of European integration, has been slammed by the opposition and even centrists in his own ruling coalition for seeking early payment of taxes by companies on severance payment funds.
In the face of this outcry the government cut the amount it had planned to raise in this way to five trillion lire from six trillion and said it would find the rest through tax amnesties.

The opposition centre-right Freedom Alliance, led by former prime minister Silvio Berlusconi, lambasted Prodi at a rally in Milan at the weekend, styling him a vampire whose high taxes were sucking the life-blood from Italy.
Prodi responded by saying he had not raised taxes excessively and insisting his policies were bearing fruit.
Italy already meets the Maastricht Treaty criteria for EMU on interest rates, inflation and exchange rates, and there was more welcome news for the government on Tuesday.
Official data showed that April inflation had fallen to 1.7 percent -- the first time the key economic indicator had dropped below 2.0 percent in 28 years.
Italy is still well wide of the EMU overall debt goal but Prodi has vowed no slackening in efforts to make the grade on the budget deficit.

His government has introduced just under 100 trillion lire of belt-tightening measures since taking office last May in a bid to cut the deficit to the key three percent of Gross Domestic Product laid down for single currency aspirants.
The ratio was 6.7 percent last year, but the government has vowed it will achieve the target in time for a decision due in May 1998 on which European Union states qualify for EMU. ($1=1,706 lire)
